blocks.text: Moreover, not only for the Syrians but also for the Arabs خلد [khuld] chuld, or chold, is the mole. This is plainly shown, to say nothing of the rest, by the descriptions of it. Alcamus [II, 438]: الخلد الغارة العميا [al-khuld al-ghāra al-ʿamyā] Alchold, the blind mouse. The book entitled الفلاحة الفارسية [al-Filāḥa al-Fārisiyya] Persian Agriculture, cited by Abenbitar: الخلد دابة عميا تحت الارض تاكل عروق الشجر ويحب رايحة البصل والكراث وتخرج من حجرتها في طلب الرايحتها [al-khuld dābba ʿamyā taḥt al-arḍ taʾkul ʿurūq al-shajar wa-yuḥibb rāyiḥat al-baṣal wa-l-kurrāth wa-takhruj min ḥujratihā fī ṭalab al-rāyiḥatihā] Alchold, a blind animal that eats the roots of trees under the ground, and that takes such delight in the smell of onion and leek ^{a)} that, lured by it, it comes out of its hiding-place ^{(4)}. And Giahid: الخلد دويبة عميا صما لا تعرف ما بين يديها الا بالشم تخرج من حجرها وهي تعلم انها لا سمع لها ولا بصر فتنفتح فاها وتقف عند حجرها فياتي الذباب فيسقط علي شدقيها ويمر بين لحييها فيستد خله جوفها بنفسها وهي تعرض لذلك في الساعات التي يكون فيها الذباب اكثر [al-khuld duwaybba ʿamyā ṣammāʾ lā taʿrif mā bayn yadayhā illā bi-l-shamm takhruj min ḥujrihā wa-hiya taʿlam annahā lā samʿ lahā wa-lā baṣar fa-tanfatiḥ fāhā wa-taqif ʿind ḥujrihā fa-yaʾtī al-dhubāb fa-yasquṭ ʿalā shidqayhā wa-yamurr bayn laḥyayhā fa-yastad khalahu jawfahā bi-nafsihā wa-hiya taʿriḍ li-dhālika fī al-sāʿāt allatī yakūn fīhā al-dhubāb akthar] Alchold is a small animal, blind and deaf, which does not recognize what is in front of it except by smell. When it comes out of its hiding-place, well aware that it lacks hearing and sight, it stands with open mouth near its hiding-place; and flies that come fall into its mouth and walk between its jaws, and are drawn by its breath into its belly. And so it opens its mouth wide at those hours when flies are most numerous. So he, who deprives الخلد [al-khuld] alchold, that is, the mole, not only of sight but also of hearing. But Damir judges otherwise; his words are: كل حيوان له عينان الا الخلد وانما خلق كذلك لانه ترابي جعل الله له الارض كالما للسمك وغذاوه في بطنها وليس له في ظاهرها قوة ولا نشاط ولما لم يكن له بصر عوضه الله حدة حاسة الشمع فيدرك الوطي [kull ḥayawān lahu ʿaynān illā al-khuld wa-innamā khuliqa ka-dhālika li-annahu turābī jaʿala Allāh lahu al-arḍ ka-l-māʾ li-l-samak wa-ghidhāʾuhu fī baṭnihā wa-laysa lahu fī ẓāhirihā quwwa wa-lā nashāṭ wa-lammā lam yakun lahu baṣar ʿawwaḍahu Allāh ḥiddat ḥāssat al-shamʿ fa-yudrik al-waṭʾ] [col. 1024] الخفي من مسافة بعيدة فانا احس بذلك جعل يحفر الارض [al-khafī min masāfa baʿīda fa-anā aḥass bi-dhālika jaʿala yaḥfur al-arḍ] Every animal has eyes except alchold, which was created without eyes, because it lives in the earth, which God assigned to it as water to the fishes, so that its food is in the belly of the earth, and outside it it lacks strength and vigour. [II, 439] But God compensated for the lack of sight by the keenness of the sense of hearing, by which it perceives even from a great distance those who walk with stealthy step; and as soon as it perceives them, it hides itself in the earth. With this agrees the statement of Pliny: Moles, though buried in the earth, so dense and deaf an element of Nature, hear more clearly. But in the opinion of some there are two kinds of mole, namely خلد [khuld] chold and زباب [zabāb] zebab, of which the former lacks sight, the latter hearing. Damir, in the chapter الفار [al-fār], that is, On the mouse: ومنها اليرابوع والزباب والخلد فالزباب صم والخلد اعمي [wa-minhā al-yarābūʿ wa-l-zabāb wa-l-khuld fa-l-zabāb ṣumm wa-l-khuld aʿmā] Among the species of mice there are also aljarbuo (or choerogryllius), zebab, and chold; of which zebab is deaf and chold blind. I could add much more, but from this it is more than sufficiently clear that for the Arabs as well as the Syrians, chold or chuld is the mole.

Third, in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Moëd Katon, ch. 1, fol. 6 b, in the words of the Mishnah צדין את האישות ואת העכברים, One may lawfully hunt moles and mice, in these words (I say) האישות, that is, the mole or moles (as all acknowledge, and as we shall show at greater length below), is rendered in the Jerusalem Talmud as חולדה chulda. I have not, indeed, read this in it myself, since the book is not at hand; but so the Gloss asserts on the passage of Moëd Katon just cited: אישות מפירש בירושלמי חולדה The word אישות is rendered in the Jerusalem Talmud as חולדה chulda. There, therefore, חולדה chulda is the mole, not the weasel.

Fourth, in Levit. XI, 29. חולד choled heads the list of those animals which are comprised under the name שרץ. Two things, moreover, are characteristic of these. One, that because of the shortness of their feet they seem to creep rather than walk. The other, that they multiply beyond measure. For this is what the verb שרץ properly signifies, and accordingly it is applied to fishes in Gen. I, 20., to frogs in Exod. VIII, 3. and Psal. CV, 30., and, καθ' ὑπερβολὴν [kath' hyperbolēn], to the Israelites in Egypt, Exod. I, 7., because in that servitude God's blessing increased their number, I might almost say, beyond all belief. Everyone knows that these marks suit weasels less than moles, whose legs are very short and whose multitude (on the authority of Pliny somewhere) is so great that they undermine whole fields.
